claim: The mercury tk256c locus was initially mapped between the SSLP markers Z20009 (G41723) and Z858 (G40668) on the distal end of chromosome 15.
source: The mercury tk256c locus (Nicolson et al., 1998) was initially mapped between the SSLP markers Z20009 (G41723) and Z858 (G40668) on the distal end of chromosome 15.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript describing the genetic mapping of the mercury locus, with citation to prior work.

claim: Sequencing of known candidate genes within the mercury critical region revealed no pathogenic mutations.
source: Sequencing of known candidate genes within this region revealed no pathogenic mutations and mRNA in situ hybridization (ISH) for these genes did not reveal any transcripts with hair cell-enriched expression patterns (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequencing experiments performed by the authors.

claim: mRNA in situ hybridization for candidate genes in the mercury critical region did not reveal any transcripts with hair cell-enriched expression patterns.
source: Sequencing of known candidate genes within this region revealed no pathogenic mutations and mRNA in situ hybridization (ISH) for these genes did not reveal any transcripts with hair cell-enriched expression patterns (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a result of ISH experiments performed by the authors.

claim: The stickleback ortholog of the human deafness gene LRTOMT/DFNB63 was present in the conserved synteny region on stickleback groupI chromosome.
source: The stickleback ortholog of the human deafness gene LRTOMT/DFNB63 was also present in this region (tomt, ENSGACG00000007832).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the presence of the tomt gene in the stickleback genome assembly.

claim: The zebrafish tomt open-reading frame was cloned and sequenced from larval RNA.
source: Using this information, we cloned and sequenced the zebrafish tomt open-reading frame (ORF) from larval RNA (Accession number KX066099).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cloning and sequencing work performed by the authors.

claim: Each mercury allele contains a nonsense mutation in the first exon of tomt.
source: Additionally, we amplified and sequenced each of the three coding exons and their flanking intronic regions from genomic DNA, and found that each mercury allele contains a nonsense mutation in the first exon of tomt (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequencing experiments and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The mercury mutations truncate the tomt protein product prior to or early within the putative O-methyltransferase domain.
source: These mutations truncate the protein product prior to (tk256c) or early within (nl16) the putative O-methyltransferase domain (Figure 1B) and are both predicted to be functional nulls.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mutation positions shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The mercury mutations are both predicted to be functional nulls.
source: These mutations truncate the protein product prior to (tk256c) or early within (nl16) the putative O-methyltransferase domain (Figure 1B) and are both predicted to be functional nulls.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the nature and position of the mutations.

claim: At 28 hpf, tomt is expressed exclusively in the presumptive anterior and posterior maculae of the developing ear.
source: (C) At 28 hpf, tomt is expressed in exclusively in the presumptive anterior (AM) and posterior (PM) maculae of the developing ear, as indicated by the white and black arrow heads respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At 4 dpf, tomt is expressed exclusively in the hair cells of the inner ear and lateral line neuromasts.
source: (E–G) At 4 dpf, tomt is expressed exclusively in the hair cells of the inner ear (F) and lateral line neuromasts (G).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in Figures 1E-G.

claim: The ISH signal for tomt is absent in tomtnl16 mutants.
source: We found that the ISH signal is absent in tomtnl16 mutants, suggesting that the G219A mutation causes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (inner ear shown Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is stated as a result of ISH experiments and shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: The G219A mutation in tomtnl16 causes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
source: We found that the ISH signal is absent in tomtnl16 mutants, suggesting that the G219A mutation causes nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (inner ear shown Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the absence of ISH signal in mutants.

claim: The tomt transcript cannot be amplified from total RNA of homozygous tomtnl16 mutants.
source: This result was confirmed using RT-PCR (Figure 1J). We were unable to amplify the tomt transcript from total RNA of homozygous tomtnl16 mutants but were still able to detect it in tomttk256c mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a result of RT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The tomt transcript can be detected in tomttk256c mutants.
source: This result was confirmed using RT-PCR (Figure 1J). We were unable to amplify the tomt transcript from total RNA of homozygous tomtnl16 mutants but were still able to detect it in tomttk256c mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a result of RT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1J.

claim: tomt is predicted to code for a single-pass membrane protein featuring a short N-terminus followed by a transmembrane domain.
source: tomt is predicted to code for a single-pass membrane protein featuring a short N-terminus followed by a transmembrane domain (TMD), with approximately 20 amino acids separating the TMD from the predicted O-methyltransferase catalytic domain.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on sequence analysis.

claim: Approximately 20 amino acids separate the TMD from the predicted O-methyltransferase catalytic domain in Tomt.
source: tomt is predicted to code for a single-pass membrane protein featuring a short N-terminus followed by a transmembrane domain (TMD), with approximately 20 amino acids separating the TMD from the predicted O-methyltransferase catalytic domain.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on sequence analysis.

claim: Immunolabel of TOMT in mouse cochlear hair cells localized the protein in the cytoplasm of inner and outer hair cells.
source: Immunolabel of TOMT in mouse cochlear hair cells localized the protein in the cytoplasm of inner and outer hair cells, and showed enrichment below the cuticular plate of OHCs (Ahmed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a result from a cited study.

claim: TOMT showed enrichment below the cuticular plate of OHCs in mouse cochlear hair cells.
source: Immunolabel of TOMT in mouse cochlear hair cells localized the protein in the cytoplasm of inner and outer hair cells, and showed enrichment below the cuticular plate of OHCs (Ahmed et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a result from a cited study.

claim: Both Tomt-GFP and Tomt-HA are enriched in an apical membrane compartment above the nucleus in zebrafish hair cells.
source: Both Tomt-GFP and Tomt-HA are enriched in an apical membrane compartment above the nucleus (Figure 2A,B), similar to immunostain for mouse TOMT.
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: No Tomt protein is detectable in the hair bundle.
source: Notably, no Tomt protein is detectable in the hair bundle.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from imaging experiments.

claim: In hair cells, the Golgi apparatus is positioned apical to the nucleus.
source: In hair cells, the Golgi apparatus is positioned apical to the nucleus (Sipe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Tomt-GFP and Mgat1a_1-110-mKate2 are partially co-localized in hair cells.
source: When co-expressed, Tomt-GFP and Mgat1a_1-110-mKate2 are partially co-localized in hair cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as a result of co-expression experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Compared to Mgat1a_1-110-mKate2, Tomt-GFP is more broadly distributed indicating that Tomt-GFP may be present at lower levels in the endoplasmic reticulum and the basolateral membrane in addition to the Golgi apparatus.
source: Compared to Mgat1a_1-110-mKate2, Tomt-GFP is more broadly distributed indicating that Tomt-GFP may be present at lower levels in the endoplasmic reticulum and the basolateral membrane in addition to the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the imaging data.

claim: The organization of Tomt's predicted protein domains is reminiscent of Golgi-resident, Type II transmembrane glycosyltransferases like Mgat1.
source: We noted that the organization of Tomt's predicted protein domains was reminiscent of Golgi-resident, Type II transmembrane glycosyltransferases like Mgat1 - a short N-terminus followed by a signal anchor TMD, and a stem region preceding the catalytic domain (Tu and Banfield, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an observation based on sequence analysis and comparison to known proteins.

claim: Tomt_1-45-GFP is enriched in the Golgi apparatus.
source: Similar to Tomt-GFP and Tomt-HA, Tomt_1-45-GFP is also enriched in the Golgi apparatus (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The first 45 amino acids of Tomt are sufficient for its subcellular localization.
source: Together, these results suggest that Tomt is a Golgi-enriched protein, and that the first 45 amino acids of Tomt are sufficient for its subcellular localization.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the localization of Tomt_1-45-GFP.

claim: Wild-type, non-transgenic siblings responded to 72% of the acoustic stimuli.
source: On average, wild-type, non-transgenic siblings responded to 72% of the acoustic stimuli (n = 20, 138/192 stimulations).
evidence: This is stated as a result of AEBR experiments.

claim: Non-transgenic mercury mutants exhibited a startle response to 2% of stimuli.
source: In contrast, non-transgenic mercury mutants exhibited a startle response to 2% of stimuli, confirming that Tomt-deficient zebrafish are deaf (n = 15; 4/177 stimulations).
evidence: This is stated as a result of AEBR experiments.

claim: Tomt-deficient zebrafish are deaf.
source: In contrast, non-transgenic mercury mutants exhibited a startle response to 2% of stimuli, confirming that Tomt-deficient zebrafish are deaf (n = 15; 4/177 stimulations).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the AEBR results.

claim: The tomt-GFP transgene can restore full auditory function to mercury mutants.
source: Strikingly, we were able to restore full auditory function to mercury mutants with the tomt-GFP transgene.
evidence: This is stated as a result of AEBR experiments with transgenic fish.

claim: The AEBR of Tg(tomt); tomttk256 larvae was statistically indistinguishable from wild-type, non-Tg and wild-type Tg(tomt) larvae.
source: The AEBR of Tg(tomt); tomttk256 larvae (n = 15; 118/158 stimulations) was statistically indistinguishable from wild-type, non-Tg and wild-type Tg(tomt) larvae (n = 18; 128/183 stimulations).
evidence: This is stated as a result of statistical analysis of AEBR data.

claim: tomt is the gene responsible for the mercury phenotype.
source: These data confirm that tomt is the gene responsible for the mercury phenotype, and indicate that the Golgi-enriched Tomt-GFP protein is fully functional and can rescue the behavioral phenotype of mercury mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: The Golgi-enriched Tomt-GFP protein is fully functional and can rescue the behavioral phenotype of mercury mutants.
source: These data confirm that tomt is the gene responsible for the mercury phenotype, and indicate that the Golgi-enriched Tomt-GFP protein is fully functional and can rescue the behavioral phenotype of mercury mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: The lateral line hair cells of mercury mutants lack microphonic currents.
source: The lateral line hair cells of mercury mutants lack microphonic currents and FM 1–43 dye uptake, both phenotypes associated with mechanotransduction defects (Nicolson et al., 1998; Seiler and Nicolson, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a result from cited studies.

claim: The lateral line hair cells of mercury mutants lack FM 1–43 dye uptake.
source: The lateral line hair cells of mercury mutants lack microphonic currents and FM 1–43 dye uptake, both phenotypes associated with mechanotransduction defects (Nicolson et al., 1998; Seiler and Nicolson, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a result from cited studies.

claim: Hair cells from the lateral line organ of wild-type and tomtnl16 mutant zebrafish showed a similar complement of K+ currents.
source: Hair cells from the lateral line organ of wild-type and tomtnl16 mutant zebrafish (3.0–5.2 dpf) showed a similar complement of K+ currents (Figure 4A,B), in agreement with that previously described for wild-type hair cells (Olt et al., 2016, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a result of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The size of the peak K+ current measured at 0 mV was similar between wild-type (261 ± 26 pA, n = 4) and mutant hair cells (352 ± 43 pA, n = 3).
source: The size of the peak K+ current measured at 0 mV was found to be similar between wild-type (261 ± 26 pA, n = 4) and mutant hair cells (352 ± 43 pA, n = 3) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a result of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In wild-type hair cells, the size of the MET current was 86 ± 35 pA (n = 4 from four zebrafish).
source: In wild-type hair cells, the size of the MET current was 86 ± 35 pA (n = 4 from four zebrafish, Figure 4D,F), with a resting open probability of the MET channel of 0.08 ± 0.03 (n = 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: The resting open probability of the MET channel in wild-type hair cells was 0.08 ± 0.03 (n = 4).
source: In wild-type hair cells, the size of the MET current was 86 ± 35 pA (n = 4 from four zebrafish, Figure 4D,F), with a resting open probability of the MET channel of 0.08 ± 0.03 (n = 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Tomt-deficient hair cells have no detectable MET current.
source: By contrast, Tomt-deficient hair cells have no detectable MET current (n = 10 from six zebrafish; Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is stated as a result of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: The peak of the Ca2+ current at –31 mV in tomtnl16 mutant hair cells was 9.2 ± 2.4 pA (n = 8).
source: The peak of the Ca2+ current at –31 mV was 9.2 ± 2.4 pA (n = 8), which was similar to that previously reported (Olt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a result of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Nascent hair cells of the lateral line organ will begin to label with FM dyes at 2 dpf.
source: Nascent hair cells of the lateral line organ will begin to label with FM dyes at 2 dpf (Figure 5A; n = 6 individuals, 2 NM each) (Kindt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 5A, with citation to prior work.

claim: Tomt-deficient hair cells did not label with FM 1–43 at 2 dpf.
source: However, Tomt-deficient hair cells did not label with FM 1–43 at this early developmental stage (n = 8 individuals, 2 NM each; Figure 5A,B), even though the neuromasts from tomttk256c mutants contained the same number of hair cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: The neuromasts from tomttk256c mutants at 2 dpf contained the same number of hair cells as wild-type.
source: However, Tomt-deficient hair cells did not label with FM 1–43 at this early developmental stage (n = 8 individuals, 2 NM each; Figure 5A,B), even though the neuromasts from tomttk256c mutants contained the same number of hair cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated as a result of hair cell counting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Wild-type neuromasts at 6 dpf contain an average of 17 hair cells per neuromast.
source: To show that the lack of functional MET channels was not a case of developmental delay, we also quantified FM 1–43 uptake at 6 dpf, a stage when wild-type neuromasts contain an average of 17 hair cells per neuromast (n = 6 individuals, 2 NM each; Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is stated as a result of hair cell counting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At 6 dpf, Tomt-deficient hair cells still did not label with FM 1–43.
source: At 6 dpf, Tomt-deficient hair cells still did not label with FM 1–43 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: At 6 dpf, there was a significant decrease in the number of hair cells per neuromast in mercury mutants (average of 13 HC / NM; n = 8 individuals, 2 NM each).
source: At this stage, we observed a significant decrease in the number of hair cells per neuromast in mercury mutants (Figure 5E, average of 13 HC / NM; n = 8 individuals, 2 NM each), consistent with what has been observed in other zebrafish mechanotransduction mutants (Seiler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a result of hair cell counting shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Injecting FM 1–43 into the ear of 6 dpf wild-type larvae led to robust labeling of inner ear hair cells.
source: Injecting FM 1–43 into the ear of 6 dpf wild-type larvae led to robust labeling of inner ear hair cells (Figure 5F, top, lateral cristae shown, n = 5).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Tomt-deficient inner ear hair cells failed to label with FM 1–43 dye.
source: However, like the lateral line organ, Tomt-deficient inner ear hair cells failed to label with FM 1–43 dye (n = 7).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments.

claim: No gross polarity defects were observed in the mercury mutant that could account for the lack of MET channel activity.
source: We did not observe any gross polarity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) or morphological defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E) that could account for the lack of MET channel activity in the mercury mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No gross morphological defects were observed in the mercury mutant that could account for the lack of MET channel activity.
source: We did not observe any gross polarity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) or morphological defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E) that could account for the lack of MET channel activity in the mercury mutant.
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tomt-deficient hair cells lack functional MET channels, even during the initial development of mechanosensitivity.
source: Together with the electrophysiological recordings in Figure 4, these data demonstrate that Tomt-deficient hair cells lack functional MET channels, even during the initial development of mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the FM dye labeling and electrophysiology data.

claim: FM 4–64 label in wild-type Tg(tomt) neuromasts was statistically identical to their wild-type, non-transgenic counterparts.
source: We observed that FM 4–64 label in wild-type Tg(tomt) neuromasts was statistically identical to their wild-type, non-transgenic counterparts (Figure 5G,H), indicating that extra Tomt protein does not appreciably alter the basal function of the MET channel.
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Extra Tomt protein does not appreciably alter the basal function of the MET channel.
source: We observed that FM 4–64 label in wild-type Tg(tomt) neuromasts was statistically identical to their wild-type, non-transgenic counterparts (Figure 5G,H), indicating that extra Tomt protein does not appreciably alter the basal function of the MET channel.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the FM dye labeling data.

claim: The lack of FM label was fully rescued in mutants stably expressing the tomt-GFP transgene specifically in hair cells.
source: The lack of FM label was fully rescued in mutants stably expressing the tomt-GFP transgene specifically in hair cells (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 5G and 5H.

claim: Full rescue of FM dye labeling was observed in a transgenic line expressing Tomt-HA.
source: We also observed full rescue of FM dye labeling in a transgenic line expressing Tomt-HA (Tg(myo6b:tomt-HA-pA); Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A cytoplasmic form of Tomt (HA-Tomt_45-259-GFP) was unable to rescue FM 4–64 label.
source: In contrast, we were unable to rescue FM 4–64 label using a cytoplasmic form of Tomt (HA-Tomt_45-259-GFP), modeled after human S-COMT (Accession # NP_009294) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C), suggesting that the putative TMD is required for Tomt function.
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The putative TMD is required for Tomt function.
source: In contrast, we were unable to rescue FM 4–64 label using a cytoplasmic form of Tomt (HA-Tomt_45-259-GFP), modeled after human S-COMT (Accession # NP_009294) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C), suggesting that the putative TMD is required for Tomt function.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the rescue experiments.

claim: The putative enzymatic portion of Tomt is required for rescue, as Tomt_1-45-GFP had no effect on FM 4–64 label in wild-type or mercury mutants.
source: Conversely, the putative enzymatic portion of Tomt is also required for rescue, as Tomt_1-45-GFP had no effect on FM 4–64 label in wild-type or mercury mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: Tomt is necessary for mechanotransduction in sensory hair cells.
source: These data suggest that Tomt is necessary for mechanotransduction in sensory hair cells, and that both the transmembrane and enzymatic domains are required.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Both the transmembrane and enzymatic domains of Tomt are required for mechanotransduction.
source: These data suggest that Tomt is necessary for mechanotransduction in sensory hair cells, and that both the transmembrane and enzymatic domains are required.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiments.

claim: The majority of neuromast hair cells are functionally mature by 5 dpf.
source: We chose a 5 dpf time point because the majority of neuromast hair cells are functionally mature by this time (Kindt et al., 2012), thereby allowing us to determine if transient expression of Tomt can restore MET to mutant hair cells that have developed without mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Prior to heat shock treatment, no distinct Tomt-GFP signal was observed.
source: Prior to heat shock treatment, no distinct Tomt-GFP signal was observed (Figure 6B,C), and little to no FM 4–64 hair cell label could be detected (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Prior to heat shock treatment, little to no FM 4–64 hair cell label could be detected.
source: Prior to heat shock treatment, no distinct Tomt-GFP signal was observed (Figure 6B,C), and little to no FM 4–64 hair cell label could be detected (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figures 6B and 6D.

claim: Post-heat shock, a significant induction of Tomt-GFP was observed.
source: Post-heat shock, we observed a significant induction of Tomt-GFP and a significant increase in FM 4–64 intensity (p<0.0001; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Post-heat shock, a significant increase in FM 4–64 intensity was observed.
source: Post-heat shock, we observed a significant induction of Tomt-GFP and a significant increase in FM 4–64 intensity (p<0.0001; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of imaging experiments shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: An acute pulse of Tomt-GFP can restore MET channel activity to previously silent hair cells within 4 hr of initiating the heat-shock treatment.
source: These results demonstrate that an acute pulse of Tomt-GFP can restore MET channel activity to previously silent hair cells, and can do so within 4 hr of initiating the heat-shock treatment.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the heat-shock experiments.

claim: Tomt plays an active role in MET channel function.
source: As such, these data suggest that Tomt plays an active role in MET channel function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the heat-shock experiments.

claim: Tomt is classed together with Catechol O-methyltransferaseCOMT in the EC 2.1.1.6 catechol O-methyltransferase protein family.
source: Tomt is classed together with Catechol O-methyltransferaseCOMT in the EC 2.1.1.6 catechol O-methyltransferase protein family (UniProt Consortium, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited source.

claim: In their enzymatic domains, Danio Tomt (amino acids 43–259) is 44% identical and 68% similar to human S-COMT (amino acids 2–221).
source: In their enzymatic domains, Danio Tomt (amino acids 43–259, Accession # ANO40802) is 44% identical and 68% similar to human S-COMT (Accession # NP_009294, amino acids 2–221) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mouse TOMT exhibited some methyltransferase activity toward norepinephrine in vitro.
source: A previous study found that mouse TOMT exhibited some methyltransferase activity toward norepinephrine in vitro (Du et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a result from a cited study.

claim: It was speculated that the deafness phenotype of the mouse mutant was caused by hair-cell degeneration resulting from a failure to properly metabolize catecholamines.
source: Based on these data, it was speculated that TOMT acts as a catechol O-methyltransferase in vivo, and that the deafness phenotype of the mouse mutant was caused by hair-cell degeneration resulting from a failure to properly metabolize catecholamines.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation from prior work.

claim: Homozygous mercury larvae expressing Comta-GFP exhibited auditory and vestibular defects identical to non-transgenic mutants.
source: Homozygous mercury larvae expressing Comta-GFP exhibited auditory and vestibular defects identical to non-transgenic mutants (data not shown), and Comta-GFP had no effect on FM 4–64 label in Tomt-deficient hair cells (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a result of behavioral and FM dye labeling experiments.

claim: Comta-GFP had no effect on FM 4–64 label in Tomt-deficient hair cells.
source: Homozygous mercury larvae expressing Comta-GFP exhibited auditory and vestibular defects identical to non-transgenic mutants (data not shown), and Comta-GFP had no effect on FM 4–64 label in Tomt-deficient hair cells (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Deficient catecholamine metabolism in hair cells is not the cause of the mercury phenotype.
source: These results suggest that deficient catecholamine metabolism in hair cells is not the cause of the mercury phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the Comta-GFP experiments.

claim: The COMT enzyme catalyses the transfer of the methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM/AdoMet) to the meta-hydroxyl group (3-O-methylation) of its catechol substrate.
source: The COMT enzyme catalyses the transfer of the methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine (SAM/AdoMet) to the meta-hydroxyl group (3-O-methylation) of its catechol substrate (Axelrod and Tomchick, 1958).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: The crystal structure for human COMT has revealed that the cluster of amino acids Asp141/191, His142/192, Trp143/193, and Lys144/194 are located in the active site.
source: The crystal structure for human COMT (structure PDB_3BWM) has revealed that the cluster of amino acids Asp141/191, His142/192, Trp143/193, and Lys144/194 are located in the active site (human S-COMT / MB-COMT amino acid numbering, Figure 8A) (Rutherford et al., 2008; Vidgren et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Asp141/191 in COMT coordinates a requisite Mg2+ ion.
source: Asp141/191 coordinates a requisite Mg2+ ion, His142/192 and Trp143/193 interact with the SAM methyl donor, while Lys144/194 interacts with the catechol substrate and may aid in catalysis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about COMT structure and function.

claim: His142/192 and Trp143/193 in COMT interact with the SAM methyl donor.
source: Asp141/191 coordinates a requisite Mg2+ ion, His142/192 and Trp143/193 interact with the SAM methyl donor, while Lys144/194 interacts with the catechol substrate and may aid in catalysis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about COMT structure and function.

claim: Lys144/194 in COMT interacts with the catechol substrate and may aid in catalysis.
source: Asp141/191 coordinates a requisite Mg2+ ion, His142/192 and Trp143/193 interact with the SAM methyl donor, while Lys144/194 interacts with the catechol substrate and may aid in catalysis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about COMT structure and function.

claim: The DHWK motif is conserved in all vertebrate COMT orthologs and some vertebrate TOMT proteins, most notably those from non-mammalian species.
source: This DHWK motif is conserved in all vertebrate COMT orthologs and some vertebrate TOMT proteins, most notably those from non-mammalian species.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis.

claim: Mammalian TOMT proteins retain only the histidine in the DHWK motif region.
source: Interestingly, mammalian TOMT proteins retain only the histidine in this region (armadillo / mouse H183 and human H216, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Mmu.TOMT-GFP can significantly restore mechanotransduction to mercury mutants.
source: Using FM 4–64 label as an assay for MET channel activity in lateral line hair cells, we find that Mmu.TOMT-GFP can significantly restore mechanotransduction to mercury mutants (p<0.0001; Figure 8B,C), albeit not to wild-type levels (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: Mmu.TOMT-GFP does not restore mechanotransduction to wild-type levels in mercury mutants.
source: Using FM 4–64 label as an assay for MET channel activity in lateral line hair cells, we find that Mmu.TOMT-GFP can significantly restore mechanotransduction to mercury mutants (p<0.0001; Figure 8B,C), albeit not to wild-type levels (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: Homozygous mercury mutants expressing Mmu.TOMT-GFP are viable, fertile, and do not exhibit obvious behavioral phenotypes.
source: However, as with the Danio Tomt-GFP transgene, homozygous mercury mutants expressing Mmu.TOMT-GFP are viable, fertile, and do not exhibit obvious behavioral phenotypes (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from behavioral analysis.

claim: TOMT-H183A can significantly rescue FM 4–64 label in mercury mutants at levels indistinguishable from wild-type mouse TOMT.
source: TOMT-H183A can significantly rescue FM 4–64 label in mercury mutants at levels indistinguishable from wild-type mouse TOMT (p<0.0001; Figure 8B,D).
evidence: This is stated as a result of FM dye labeling experiments shown in Figures 8B and 8D.

claim: Homozygous mercury mutants with the TOMT-H183A transgene are viable, fertile, and do not exhibit obvious behavioral phenotypes.
